steps.say: Some subdurals declare themselves on day one, but the chronic kind hides for weeks. An elderly patient who drifts in and out of alertness after a forgotten knock needs a scan.
steps.tx: **Chronic subdural haematoma** (old surface clot) follows minor trauma weeks earlier in elderly, alcoholic or anticoagulated patients, when a liquefied clot with inner and outer **neomembranes** (new vessel walls) and fragile vessels **rebleeds** (bleeds again) repeatedly into the collection, slowly expanding the crescent until pressure symptoms appear.

vis.alt: Diagram of crescentic chronic subdural haematoma with bridging veins and midline shift.
vis.caption: Chronic subdural haematoma: crescentic clot, torn bridging veins and shift. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Families report fluctuation, not coma. Weakness that comes and goes, or seizures weeks after a fall, should trigger imaging.
steps.tx: Presentation is fluctuating consciousness, headache, **hemiparesis** (one sided weakness) or new seizures rather than coma, and **bilateral collections** (clots on both sides) can cause paradoxical quadriparesis with a deceptively good **Glasgow Coma Scale** (consciousness score), while families often report personality change before weakness is noticed.

steps.say: Density tells the age of the clot. Grey brain density at two to three weeks is the easiest stage to miss on CT.
steps.tx: CT shows a crescent that is hypodense when old, **isodense** (same shade as brain) at **2 to 3 weeks** (two to three weeks) when easiest to miss, and mixed density with **septations** (dividing walls) when membranes and fresh blood coexist in one collection.

steps.say: Two small holes wash it out. A drain left for a day or two halves the chance the collection returns.
steps.tx: Symptomatic or thick collections with shift are washed out through one or two frontal-parietal **burr holes** (skull drill openings) with warm saline irrigation, and a closed **subdural drain** (tube drain) for **24 to 48 hours** (one to two days) halves recurrence compared with washout alone.

vis.alt: Coronal diagram of torn bridging vein with crescentic subdural haematoma, shift and head CT.
vis.caption: Torn bridging vein feeding a crescentic subdural with midline shift. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Frail patients get the bedside option while organised clots need full surgery. Membranes decide the approach.
steps.tx: **Twist-drill drainage** (bedside needle washout) suits frail high-risk patients while craniotomy with **membranectomy** (membrane removal) is reserved for **organised subdural** (solid scarred clot), calcified or multiply recurrent collections with solid membranes, and the choice is revisited when the first washout leaves septated residue on scan.

steps.say: Blocking the membrane blood supply cuts recurrence. Embolisation has become the standard add-on for problem collections.
steps.tx: **Middle meningeal artery embolisation** (membrane vessel closure) devascularises the outer membrane and is now the standard adjunct for recurrent, bilateral or high-risk surgical collections after the **EMBOLISE** (embolisation trial) and **STEM** (embolisation trial) trial readouts, with particles or liquid embolic delivered through the frontal and parietal branches.

steps.say: Steroids harm here despite old habits. The Dex trial showed worse function with dexamethasone, so it stays out of routine care.
steps.tx: Routine **dexamethasone** (steroid drug) is avoided after **Dex-CSDH** (steroid trial) showed worse functional outcomes with steroids, and routine statins or **tranexamic acid** (clot steadying drug) are not first-line outside trials for chronic collections, though short seizure cover follows any witnessed fit in elderly patients.

steps.say: Recovery needs air out and blood moving again. Flat positioning for a day, early walking and quick restart of thinners balance the two risks.
steps.tx: Postoperative **pneumocephalus** (trapped head air) settles with a flat head-end for a day, early mobilisation, prompt drain removal and resumption of **anticoagulation** (blood thinner) within days balance recurrence against **thromboembolism** (clot elsewhere) in elderly patients, and a follow-up scan at six weeks confirms the brain has re-expanded.
